dataset.name: JavaScript Fundamentals
dataset.description: JavaScript basics: types and coercion, arrays, functions and scope, objects and classes, async code and modern syntax.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explanation: let is block-scoped and reassignable. const is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned, and var is function-scoped.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(typeof null);
questions.explanation: typeof null returns "object". This is a long-standing quirk of the language kept for backward compatibility.

questions.question: Declaring an object with const prevents you from changing the object's properties.
questions.explanation: const prevents reassigning the variable, but the object it points to can still be modified. Object.freeze prevents property changes.

questions.question: The ______ operator compares two values for equality without performing type coercion.
questions.explanation: === is strict equality and returns false if the types differ, while == converts types before comparing.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);
questions.explanation: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floating point values, so 0.1 + 0.2 has a tiny rounding error.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log("5" + 3, "5" - 3);
questions.explanation: With +, a string operand makes it concatenation ("5" + 3 is "53"). The - operator always converts to numbers, so "5" - 3 is 2.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([] + {});
questions.explanation: Both operands are converted to strings: [] becomes "" and {} becomes "[object Object]", then they are concatenated.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined);
questions.explanation: == treats null and undefined as equal to each other, but === also compares types, and they are different types.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(NaN === NaN);
questions.explanation: NaN is the only JavaScript value that is not equal to itself. Use Number.isNaN to test for it.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(typeof NaN);
questions.explanation: NaN stands for "not a number" but its type is still number.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(1 < 2 < 3, 3 > 2 > 1);
questions.explanation: 1 < 2 is true, and true < 3 becomes 1 < 3, which is true. 3 > 2 is true, and true > 1 becomes 1 > 1, which is false.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([10, 9, 1].sort());
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares them alphabetically, so "10" comes before "9".

questions.question: Which array method adds an element to the end of the array?
questions.explanation: push appends to the end. pop removes the last element, shift removes the first, and unshift adds to the front.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log("hello".toUpperCase());
questions.explanation: toUpperCase returns a new uppercase string.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0));
questions.explanation: filter keeps the elements for which the callback returns true, here the even numbers.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2));
questions.explanation: map returns a new array with the callback applied to every element.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));
questions.explanation: reduce combines all elements into one value. Starting at 0, it adds 1, 2, 3 and 4.
The spread operator copies a's elements into a new array and adds 4. The original a is unchanged.

questions.question: Array.prototype.map modifies the original array in place.
questions.explanation: map returns a new array and leaves the original unchanged.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log("a-b-c".split("-").join("+"));
questions.explanation: split breaks the string into an array on "-", and join glues the pieces back together with "+".

questions.question: The array method ______ removes and returns the last element.
questions.explanation: pop removes the last element. shift removes the first.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([1, 2, 3].indexOf(4), [NaN].includes(NaN), [NaN].indexOf(NaN));
questions.explanation: includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN. indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN === NaN is false, so it finds nothing.
Setting length to a smaller number truncates the array.

questions.question: In JavaScript, arrays are a separate primitive type, not objects.
questions.explanation: Arrays are objects. typeof [] returns "object", and Array.isArray is used to tell arrays apart from other objects.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid arrow function that returns the sum of a and b?
questions.explanation: Arrow functions use =>. An expression after the arrow is returned automatically.
var declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined, but the assignment of 5 happens later.
let variables are hoisted but cannot be accessed before their declaration (the temporal dead zone), which throws a ReferenceError.
The returned arrow function closes over c, so the count persists between calls. The third call returns 3.
When b is not passed, its default value 2 is used. f(1) gives 3, and f(1, 5) gives 6.

questions.question: What does IIFE stand for?
questions.explanation: An IIFE is a function that is defined and called right away, such as (function () { ... })(). It is often used to create a private scope.
var is function-scoped, so all three closures share one i. By the time they run, the loop has ended with i equal to 3.
let creates a new binding for each loop iteration, so each closure captures its own value of i.
Function declarations are hoisted together with their body. The var f declaration adds nothing new, and the assignment f = 1 has not run yet.

questions.question: Arrow functions have their own this binding, just like regular functions.
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not create their own this. They use the this of the surrounding scope.

questions.question: Which syntax reads a property whose name is stored in a variable called key?
questions.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates the expression inside the brackets. obj.key would look for a property literally named "key".
The pattern takes a from the object. For b: c = 5, the property b is missing, so the default value 5 is used for c.
With spread, later properties override earlier ones, so y becomes 3.

questions.question: Object.freeze makes an object deeply immutable, including nested objects.
questions.explanation: Object.freeze is shallow. Nested objects can still be changed unless they are frozen too.

questions.question: What is the name of the method that initializes a new instance of a JavaScript class?
questions.explanation: A class defines its initialization logic in the constructor method, which runs when new is used.
super.hi() calls the parent class's method, which returns "A", and "B" is appended.
In the regular method, this is the object, so this.n is "obj". The arrow function takes this from the enclosing scope, not from o, so this.n is undefined.
Calling f() as a plain function loses the object, so this is no longer o (it is the global object, or undefined in strict mode), and the result is undefined.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(JSON.stringify({a: [1, {b: 2}], c: undefined}));
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify omits properties whose value is undefined.

questions.question: JavaScript classes are syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance.
questions.explanation: The class syntax is a cleaner way to write constructor functions and prototype chains. The underlying model is still prototypal.

questions.question: Which built-in object represents a value that will be available in the future (or an error)?
questions.explanation: A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation and is either pending, fulfilled or rejected.
Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Then the microtask queue (promise callbacks) runs before the timer callback, so C comes before B.

questions.question: Using await inside a regular (non-async) function is a syntax error.
questions.explanation: await is allowed only inside async functions (and at the top level of ES modules).
An async function always returns a Promise, even if it returns a plain value.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject("x"), Promise.resolve(3)])
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(e => console.log("err", e));
questions.explanation: Promise.all rejects as soon as any promise rejects, so the catch handler runs with the reason "x".
The function runs synchronously until await, printing 1. At await it pauses and returns to the caller, which prints 3. The rest of the function (2) resumes afterwards.

questions.question: The ______ method of a promise registers a handler for when the promise is rejected.
questions.explanation: promise.catch(handler) handles rejections and is equivalent to then(undefined, handler).
Timers run after the current synchronous code, in order of their delay. The 0 ms timer fires before the 10 ms one.

questions.question: JavaScript runs your code on multiple threads at once, so two callbacks can execute at exactly the same time.
questions.explanation: JavaScript uses a single-threaded event loop. Callbacks run one at a time, though asynchronous work such as I/O can proceed in the background.

questions.question: Which characters delimit a template literal in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: Template literals use backticks and support interpolation with ${...} and multi-line strings.
The empty slot between the commas skips the second element, so a is 1 and b is 3.
Optional chaining stops and returns undefined if a part of the chain is null or undefined, instead of throwing.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(0 ?? 5, 0 || 5);
questions.explanation: ?? only falls back for null or undefined, so 0 is kept. || falls back for any falsy value, so 0 || 5 is 5.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log([...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3])]);
questions.explanation: A Set removes duplicates, and spreading it turns it back into an array.
After set, the Map has two entries, and get("b") returns 2.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following code?

console.log(Array.from({length: 3}, (_, i) => i * 2));
questions.explanation: Array.from accepts an array-like object ({ length: 3 }) and a mapping function. The mapper receives the index i, so the result is 0, 2, 4.
Symbols are a primitive type, and every Symbol() call creates a unique value, even with the same description.

questions.question: A for...of loop over a plain object iterates over its property names.
questions.explanation: for...of works on iterables (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets) and a plain object is not iterable, so it throws a TypeError. for...in iterates over property names.

questions.question: let and const declarations are hoisted, but cannot be used before their declaration line runs.
questions.explanation: They exist from the start of their scope but are in the temporal dead zone until the declaration executes.
